newsitem.title: UK: LME copper stocks surge, more seen in pipeline.
newsitem.headline: LME copper stocks surge, more seen in pipeline.

text.p: A hefty rise in London Metal Exchange (LME) copper stocks on Wednesday heralds increasing deliveries into warehouses as the market moves from a short-term supply squeeze into surplus, analysts said.
Some of the metal was sucked in by near-term technical tightness which sent the premium of cash metal over three months delivery material surging to $270 on Tuesday.
The stocks rise, however, was also a result of long-expected deliveries from the Far East as well as arbitrage business between the LME and Comex, they added.

In the long term, stocks will continue to mount as new mines churn out more metal than can be absorbed by consumers, many analysts said. Bulls, however, believe China will go on a buying spree later this year and soak up excess material.
LME stocks shot up on Wednesday by 17,025 tonnes to 160,325 tonnes, with the largest chunk appearing in the Singapore warehouse, at about a net 7,500 tonnes.
Around 6,000 tonnes were delivered into U.S. warehouses and the rest scattered among a wide range of locations.
Stocks have been rising since bottoming at 121,550 tonnes on June 20, but on most days increases have been a few thousand tonnes.
"This certainly unsettled the market...and I think there is more to come," said analyst Angus MacMillan of broker Billiton.
Three month prices slumped to a low of $2,247 in pre-market trading on Wednesday from Tuesday's afternoon kerb close of $2,278.
The technical tightness which has sent players scrambling to cover short positions will continue to pull metal out of the woodwork over the next two weeks.
"People are quite keen to take advantage of the backwardation," said analyst William Adams of broker Rudolf Wolff. "There is talk of more large deliveries of metal appearing."
Some of the metal that ended up in LME depots in the U.S. originated from Comex warehouses, as players took advantage of arbitrage opportunities, analysts said.
On Tuesday, Comex copper inventories declined by 1,321 short tons.
The market was not bothered if metal was merely being transferred from Comex to LME warehouses, but there appears to be a net build up of material as U.S. demand slows down slightly, MacMillan said.
Large deliveries of metal into the Singapore warehouse had been expected over the past few weeks from China, Korea and Taiwan, analysts said.
Slow demand in Asia and high LME prices had spurred the movements, Adams said.

Last month, South Korea's LG Metals Corp said it had sold about 10,000 tonnes of copper, supplied by Chile's Codelco, to European metal firm Metallgesellschaft. Trade souces said the metal would be sent to Singapore in late June or early July.
If the metal came from China, it would cast a pall over optimistic forecasts for up to 300,000 tonnes of Chinese buying this year, said analyst Nick Moore of Flemings Global Mining Group.
"That would be one in the eye for the copper bulls," he said.
Flemings is forecasting the market to flip from deficit into a surplus of 130,000 tonnes this year, rising to a surplus of 500,000 tonnes by the year 2000.
Prices are forecast to decline from an average of $1.10 per lb ($2,425 per tonne) this year to 80 cents/lb ($1,764/tonne) by 2000, Moore added.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
